prompt: Which idea can be tested as it is written?

options.text: Stocks with a good feeling are the best ones to hold.
Stocks that close above their 55-day high have a higher average result after costs than other stocks over the test period. The idea is dropped if the average result after costs is not above zero.
Strong markets are good for trading.
This idea has a name, so it is testable.

explanations.a: A feeling has no number. No result could prove it wrong, so it cannot be tested as written.
explanations.c: Strong and good have no measurable meaning here. The idea needs an entry, an exit and a number that defines a pass.
explanations.d: A name does not make an idea testable. The idea needs a rule that a result could contradict.

prompt: After a test shows a small loss, you change the pass rule so the idea now passes. What have you done?

options.text: Normal refinement, because you learned something from the result.
Created a different, untested idea, because the rule changed after the results were seen.
Run a fair test, because the change was small.
Proved that the original idea works.

explanations.a: Learning from a result is good, but the rule must not move to fit that result. The change makes the test unfair.
explanations.c: A small change to a rule after results is still a change after results. The first test already said not supported.
explanations.d: Moving the pass rule proves nothing about the original idea. The first result stands.

prompt: A backtest on old prices shows a profit. What does this result show?

options.text: The idea works.
The idea passed one test under its rules, which is weak evidence.
The idea will make money with real money.
The rule can be traded safely with Rs 50,000.

explanations.a: One test under one set of rules does not prove that an idea works.
explanations.c: Old prices cannot show what will happen with real money. Real trading adds costs, slippage and changing markets.
explanations.d: A test result does not make any rule safe. Safety comes from limits on loss, not from one test.

prompt: A teammate shows you a chart and says, this pattern always works. What should you do first?

options.text: Trade a small position to see what happens.
Write the hypothesis, the entry, the exit and the pass rule before any test.
Post the chart as a proven setup for the group.
Ask for more charts before deciding anything.

explanations.a: Trading to see what happens uses real money before the idea is tested. That is not a test plan.
explanations.c: A chart shown with a claim is not proof. Calling it proven is wrong until it has a written test.
explanations.d: More charts add more ideas to test. They do not make this idea testable.

prompt: Here is a plan: Buy at the next open after a close above the 55-day high. Exit when the trade feels extended. Which part is wrong?

options.text: The entry, because it uses a close.
The exit, because feels extended is a feeling with no rule.
The 55-day high, because it cannot be measured.
Nothing is wrong, the plan is complete.

explanations.a: The entry is measurable. A close and a next open can be checked on past data.
explanations.c: The 55-day high can be measured from the price data, so it is not the problem.
explanations.d: The plan still has no stop, no sizing and no pass rule. Its exit cannot be checked either.

prompt: Hypothetical. Capital is Rs 50,000 and the risk per trade is 1%. How many rupees can one trade risk?
solution: Risk budget = 1% x Rs 50,000 = 0.01 x 50,000 = Rs 500. Check: Rs 50,000 divided by 100 is Rs 500.
